svg.title: How a function reaches Dataverse with a managed identity
svg.desc: Four steps from left to right. One: the function code asks its credential object for a token for the scope https://cedar-dev.crm.dynamics.com/.default; there is no secret in code or settings, only the client ID of the user-assigned identity id-cedar-ops-dev. Two: the Azure platform's identity endpoint inside the function app vouches for the app and Microsoft Entra ID issues an access token whose application ID is the identity's client ID. Three: the function sends the token as a bearer token to Dataverse. Four: Dataverse finds the application user whose application ID equals that client ID, named Cedar Operations, and checks its security role Operations Health – Cedar. Below, three columns compare credentials: client secret (a text that expires, must be stored, rotated and can leak), certificate (a private key that must be stored and rotated), managed identity (nothing to store, rotate or leak; exists only in Azure; assigned to resources). A second row shows the same idea for the other connections of the app: host storage through AzureWebJobsStorage__accountName, the queue through OpsStorage__queueServiceUri, telemetry through an authentication string, each with a role assignment instead of a key. A last box: on a developer machine there is no managed identity; DefaultAzureCredential uses the developer's own sign-in, so local runs act as the developer.
